x: Commentary on Surah “A Questioner Asked.” In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.
Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted:
h

A questioner asked about a punishment bound to occur (1), for the unbelievers, which none can repel (2), from God, Lord of the ascending ways (3). The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years (4). So be patient with gracious patience (5).
Abū Jaʿfar said: The readers differed in how they read His saying, “A questioner asked.”
Most of the readers of Kūfah and Baṣrah read it with a hamzah, “saʾala sāʾil” (“a questioner asked”), meaning that one of the unbelievers asked about the punishment of God and whom it would befall.

Some of the readers of Madīnah read it without a hamzah, “sāla sāʾil,” construing it as a form derived from flowing. The more correct of the two readings is the one with the hamzah, because the authoritative body of readers agrees on it, and most of the early authorities on interpretation understood it with the hamzah. We mention those who interpreted it that way and explained it in a sense like ours.

m: concerning His saying, “So be patient with gracious patience”: This was when He commanded him to pardon them and not retaliate. When he was then commanded to fight and treat them harshly, he was commanded to be severe and fight them until they abandoned it; this command was abrogated. Ibn Zayd’s claim that this verse first commanded pardon and was then abrogated has no sound basis. There is no evidence supporting his claim by any of the means by which claims are established. God’s command to His Prophet to be patiently forbearing in the face of the polytheists’ abuse does not require that this command applied only in some circumstances. Rather, God commanded him to do so in all circumstances: from the time God sent him until He took him, he continued to suffer their abuse and remained patient with it, both before God permitted him to fight them and after He permitted him to do so.

God, exalted is His mention, says that these polytheists consider the punishment they asked about, which is to befall them, far off. He, glorified is His praise, informed us that they consider it far off because they did not believe in it and denied resurrection after death, reward, and punishment. Thus He says: They consider it not destined to occur, whereas We see it as near, because it is coming; everything that is coming is near. The pronouns in “they” refer to the unbelievers, and the pronoun in “see it” refers to the punishment.

x: Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted:
h
No indeed! It is the Blaze (15), stripping away the scalp (16), calling whoever turned away and withdrew (17), and amassed wealth and hoarded it.
God, exalted is His mention, says: No, the matter is not as they imagine; nothing will save him from God’s punishment.

He then began to report what He, glorified is His praise, has prepared there for him, saying: “It is the Blaze.” Laẓā is one of the names of Hell, which is why it is not declined. Grammarians differed about its grammatical position. Some grammarians of Baṣrah said that it is in the accusative as an appositive to the pronoun, and that the predicate of “inna” is “stripping away.” He said: If you wish, you may make “Laẓā” nominative as the predicate of “inna,” and make “stripping away” nominative as a new clause. One of those who objected to this said: An explicit noun should not be made appositive to an implicit pronoun except in anomalous usage. He said that the preferred reading is: “It is the Blaze, stripping away the scalp,” with “the Blaze” as the predicate and “stripping away” as a circumstantial accusative. He said: Whoever reads it nominative begins a new clause, since it is praise or blame; it cannot begin otherwise.

In our view, the correct position is that “the Blaze” is the predicate and “stripping away” begins a new clause, which is why it is nominative. The accusative is not permissible in recitation, since the readers of the cities unanimously read it nominative and no reader recited it in the accusative (1), even though the accusative is grammatically possible. It is also possible that the pronoun in “it is” is an anticipatory pronoun, with “the Blaze” nominative and “stripping away” its predicate, as in “It is Hind standing”; in either analysis the pronoun is anticipatory. His saying, “stripping away the scalp”: God, exalted is His mention, informs us that the Blaze tears away the skin of the head and the extremities of the body. Al-shawā is the plural of shawāh, a part of the human body that is not fatal. One says, “He shot and struck only the extremities,” when he did not strike a fatal part.

And those who guard their private parts (29), except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy (30). But whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors (31).
God, exalted is His mention, says: “Those who guard their private parts” means their sexual organs.

They guard them from every use God has forbidden, but they are not blameworthy for not guarding them from their wives or from the slave women whom their right hands possess. It is said that the phrase “who guard their private parts (29), except from their wives” has no preceding negation. The wording “for then they are not blameworthy” indicates that a negation is understood in the passage. This is like someone saying: “Do whatever you wish, except commit a sin, for you will be punished for it”; that means: Do whatever you wish, except that you will be punished for committing a sin.

His saying, “But whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors”: Whoever seeks a sexual partner for his private parts other than his wife or a woman whom his right hand possesses, those people are the transgressors. They have crossed from what God made lawful for them into what He made unlawful, and so they are blameworthy.
Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted:
h

And those who are attentive to their trusts and their covenant (32), and those who uphold their testimonies (33), and those who carefully maintain their prayer (34)—those will be honored in gardens (35).

God, exalted is His mention, says: And except those who observe the trusts God has entrusted to them—His obligations—and the trusts of His servants entrusted to them, as well as His covenants imposed on them to obey His commands and prohibitions, and the covenants His servants made with them according to what He bound Himself to do for them.

They watch over and preserve these trusts and covenants without neglecting them; rather, they fulfill them and take care of them as God obligated and required. “And those who uphold their testimonies”: He says: Those who do not conceal what they have been called to testify about, but give their testimony when required, without altering or changing it. “And those who carefully maintain their prayer”: He says: Those who maintain the appointed times of the prayers God prescribed for them and their required limits, neither neglecting their times nor their limits.
His saying, “those will be honored in gardens”: God, mighty and exalted, says: Those who do these deeds will be honored in gardens, where God will honor them with His generosity.
Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted:
h

So what is the matter with those who disbelieve, rushing toward you (36), to the right and to the left in groups (37)? Does each one of them expect to be admitted into a garden of bliss (38)? No indeed! We created them from what they know (39).
God, exalted is His mention, says: What is the matter with those who disbelieve in God, rushing toward you, O Muḥammad?
We have already explained the meaning of “rushing” and what the authorities on interpretation said about it, with evidence sufficient to make repetition unnecessary here
n
, but we will mention in this passage some reports we did not cite there.

m: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd related to us: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say concerning “in groups”: In circles and companies.

c: Yūnus told me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd said
m: concerning “to the right and to the left in groups”: A group is a gathering of three or four people; gatherings of three or four are groups.

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us: Muʾammal related to us: Sufyān related to us
m: n
, from ʿAbd al-Malik b. ʿUmayr, from Abū Salamah, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet came out to his Companions while they were sitting in circles and said: “Why do I see you sitting in groups?”

m: Rāfiʿ, from Tamīm b. Ṭarafah al-Ṭāʾī, from Jābir b. Samurah, who said: The Messenger of God came to us while we were scattered, and said: “Why are they sitting in groups?”
n

c: ʿAbd Allāh b. Muḥammad b. ʿAmr al-Ghazzī told me: al-Firyābī related to us: Sufyān related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Musayyib b.
m: Rāfiʿ, from Tamīm b. Ṭarafah, from Jābir b. Samurah, who said: The Prophet came to some of his Companions while they were sitting and said: “Why do I see you sitting in circles, in groups?”
n

m: Rāfiʿ, from Tamīm b. Ṭarafah, from Jābir b. Samurah, who said: The Prophet came to some of his Companions while they were sitting and said: “Why do I see you sitting in circles, in groups?” (4).

m: Rāfiʿ, from Tamīm b. Ṭarafah al-Ṭāʾī, who said: Jābir b. Samurah related to us that the Prophet came out to them while they were sitting in circles and said: “Why do I see you sitting in groups?”—meaning in circles. This refers to His saying, “to the right and to the left in groups.”

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us: Abū ʿĀmir related to us: Qurrah related to us, from al-Ḥasan,
m: concerning His saying, “to the right and to the left in groups.” He said: “Groups” means dispersed; they go off to the right and the left, saying, “What did this man say?”
n

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us: Ḥammād b. Masʿadah related to us: Qurrah related to us, from al-Ḥasan,
m: with the same wording. The singular of ʿizīn is ʿizah, just as the singular of thibīn is thibah, and the singular of kurīn is kurah. The camel-herder’s verse also uses ʿizīn
n
: “O successor of the Merciful, my clan—its herds at dusk are scattered in remnants, sitting in groups.”

x: His saying, “Does each one of them expect to be admitted into a garden of bliss?” He says: Does each one of these unbelievers rushing toward you expect that God will admit him into “a garden of bliss”—that is, gardens in which he will enjoy bliss? The readers differed in how they read His saying, “to be admitted into a garden of bliss.” Most of the readers of the cities read “to be admitted” with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, as a passive verb. Al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥah b. Muṣarrif are reported to have read it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ
n

, meaning: Does each one of them expect that each one of them will enter a garden of bliss? In our view, the correct reading is the one followed by the readers of the cities, with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, because the authoritative body of readers agrees on it.

evidence.text: The readers differed in how they read His saying, “to be admitted into a garden of bliss.”
Most of the readers of the cities read “to be admitted” with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, as a passive verb.
Al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥah b. Muṣarrif are reported to have read it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ (3), meaning: Does each one of them expect that each one of them will enter a garden of bliss?
In our view, the correct reading is the one followed by the readers of the cities, with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, because the authoritative body of readers agrees on it.

x: His saying, “No indeed! We created them from what they know”: God, mighty and exalted, says: The matter is not as these unbelievers expect—that each one of them will be admitted into a garden of bliss.

His saying, “No indeed! We created them from what they know”: He, mighty and exalted, says: We created them from filthy semen. The one among them who deserves to enter the Garden deserves it through obedience, not merely by virtue of having been created. How can they expect to enter the Garden while they are disobedient unbelievers?

c: Bishr related to us: Yazīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah,
m: concerning His saying, “We created them from what they know.” He said: You were created from something filthy, son of Adam, so be mindful of God
n

x: Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted:
h

So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests: We are surely able (40) to replace them with better than them, and We cannot be outdone (41). So leave them to indulge and play until they meet the Day they have been promised (42).
God, exalted is His mention, says: I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests: “We are surely able (40) to replace them with better than them.”

He says: We are surely able to destroy them and bring forth better creatures than them, who obey Me and do not disobey Me. “And We cannot be outdone”: God, exalted is His mention, says: No one among them can escape what We intend for him and thereby elude Us. The authorities on interpretation said much the same as we have said. We mention who said this.

c: Yaʿqūb b. Ibrāhīm told me: Ibn ʿUlayyah related to us: ʿUmārah b. Abī Ḥafṣah informed us, from ʿIkrimah, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās said:
m: The sun rises each year through three hundred and sixty windows. Each day it rises through one window, and does not return to that window until the same day of the following year. It rises only reluctantly, saying: My Lord, do not make me rise upon Your servants, for I see them disobeying You and committing sins. He said: Have you not heard the words of Umayyah b. Abī al-Ṣalt
n
, “until it is dragged and flogged”? I said: O my master, is the sun flogged? He replied: May your father’s genitals bite you! The poet was forced by the rhyme to say “flogged”
n

c: Ibn al-Muthannā related to us: Ibn ʿUmārah related to me: ʿUmārah informed us, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning God’s saying, “by the Lord of the easts and the wests.” He said: The sun rises through three hundred and sixty places of rising; each day it rises from a place it will not return to until the following year, and it rises only reluctantly. ʿIkrimah said: I told him that the poet had said, “until it is dragged and flogged.” Ibn ʿAbbās replied: May your father’s genitals bite you! The rhyme forced him to say it.

c: Khallād b. Aslam related to us: al-Naḍr informed us: Shuʿbah informed us: ʿUmārah informed us, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: that the sun rises through three hundred and sixty windows, and when it has risen through one window, it does not rise through it again until the following year; it rises only reluctantly
n

c: Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: My father related to me; my uncle related to me; my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning His saying, “So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests.” He said: It refers to the places where the sun and the moon rise and set
n

x: His saying, “So leave them to indulge and play”: He says to His Prophet Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him: Leave these polytheists who rush toward you, scattered to the right and the left in groups, to indulge in their falsehood and play in this world, “until they meet the Day they have been promised.” He says: Until they meet the punishment of the Day of Resurrection that they have been promised.
Discussion of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted:
h
On the Day when they emerge from the graves swiftly, as if racing toward a standing marker (43), their eyes humbled, humiliation overwhelming them. That is the Day they were promised (44).

His saying, “on the Day when they emerge”: This explains and clarifies the earlier “Day” in His saying, “the Day they have been promised.” The passage means: until they meet the Day they have been promised—the Day when they emerge from the graves. A grave is called jadath, plural ajdāth. “Swiftly, as if racing toward a standing marker.”

c: Bishr related to us: Yazīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah,
m: concerning “on the Day when they emerge from the graves swiftly.” He said: Swiftly from the graves
n

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah,
m: with the same wording (3). We have already explained the word jadath, with supporting evidence and what the scholars said about it
n

x: His saying, “as if racing toward a standing marker”: He says: As if they were racing toward a marker set up for them. The readers of the cities unanimously read the nūn in naṣb with a fatḥah; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have read it with a ḍammah together with the ṣād
n

. Those who read it with a fatḥah construe naṣb as a verbal noun from the expression “I set up the thing,” meaning: as if they were hastening toward an erected idol. Those who read it with a ḍammah construe it as singular of anṣāb, the idols they worshipped. As for His saying, “racing,” ifāḍah means hurrying. A poet said
n
: “I will describe a swift ostrich, gray-backed, setting out at dawn in search of shelter.” That is, it seeks a refuge to which it can turn; ifāḍah means speed. Ruʾbah also said
n
: “Our earnest purpose goes on at evening, in haste.” The authorities on interpretation said much the same as we have said.
We mention who said this.

m: concerning this verse, “as if racing toward a standing marker”: Toward signs, racing
n

c: Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: My father related to me; my uncle related to me; my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning His saying, “as if racing toward a standing marker.” He said: Toward a marker, hurrying (1).
Muḥammad b. ʿAmr told me: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us: ʿĪsā related to us.

c: Al-Ḥārith also told me: al-Ḥasan related to us: Warqāʾ related to us,
m: both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, concerning His saying, “as if racing toward a standing marker.” He said: Racing
n

c: Bishr related to us: Yazīd related to us: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah,
m: concerning it. He said: Toward a marker, hurrying.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah,
m: concerning “as if racing toward a standing marker.” He said: Toward a marker; “racing” means hurrying
n

c: ʿAlī b. Sahl related to us: al-Walīd b. Muslim related to us:
m: I heard Abū ʿAmr
n
say: I heard Yaḥyā b. Abī Kathīr say concerning “as if racing toward a standing marker”: Toward a finish line, racing
n

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn:
m: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd related to us: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say concerning His saying, “as if racing toward a standing marker”: Toward a marker, setting off.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us: Mihrān related to us, from Sufyān,
m: concerning “racing toward a standing marker.” He said: Toward a marker, competing in a race.

c: Yūnus told me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd said
m: concerning His saying, “as if racing toward a standing marker.” He said: The anṣāb were stones they worshipped—tall stones called nuṣub. Concerning His saying, “racing,” he said: They hurry toward it as people hurry toward an idol, racing. Ibn Zayd said: The anṣāb were the idols the people of the pre-Islamic age worshipped, visited, and revered. One of them would carry an idol with him; when he saw one more beautiful, he would take it and throw the first away. God said of it: “A burden to its master: wherever he directs it, it brings no good. Is he equal to one who commands justice and is on a straight path?”
n

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us: Abū ʿĀmir related to us: Qurrah related to us, from al-Ḥasan,
m: concerning His saying, “as if racing toward a standing marker.” He said: They race to their idols, each trying to be the first to touch it
n

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us: Ḥammād b. Masʿadah related to us: Qurrah related to us, from al-Ḥasan,
m: with the same wording.
